documents: Published paper PDF: Deyong et al., Free water input into the New Britain subduction zone in Solomon Sea estimated from reflected seismic data, Geophysical Prospecting 73:735-751

entry.evidence: Quantitative estimation of the fluid flux of a subduction system is of great significance for assessing the balance of fluid

steps.action: Pose the aim of quantitatively estimating the pore-water flux into the New Britain subduction zone, noting that earlier impedance work in the area was qualitative and S-wave based.
steps.quote: Quantitative estimation of the fluid flux of a subduction system is of great significance

steps.action: Use long-streamer 2D seismic line 200 (collected 2017, 10,050 m streamer, processed by DownUnder GeoSolutions through pre-stack time migration and stack).
steps.quote: The data were processed using DownUnder GeoSolutions.

steps.action: Take velocity, density and porosity logs from eight ODP/IODP holes and the L'Etoile No. 1 industry well.
steps.quote: Nine drilling holes were used in this study

steps.action: Interpret horizons manually to build a 13-layer stratigraphic framework, using Miura et al. (2004) thicknesses and dividing the basalt evenly into layers for lack of information.
steps.quote: the interior of the basalt strata is evenly divided into several layers.

steps.action: Adopt constrained sparse spike inversion (Jason Workbench), an oil-and-gas reservoir method rarely used on large-scale seismic data, for P-impedance inversion.
steps.quote: this method is rarely applied to large-scale seismic data. In this study, we attempted to use this method

steps.action: Tie the L'Etoile No. 1 well to the seismic data with synthetic seismograms, check the cross-correlation and extract the wavelet (Figure 5).
steps.quote: Figure 5 presents the matching of synthetic seismic and real seismic data

steps.action: Build a low-frequency model from smoothed processing interval velocities with Gardner densities to cover missing deep logs, then invert for the P-wave impedance profile (Figures 6 and 7).
steps.quote: this study introduced a smoothed interpolation velocity model corresponding to the seismic profile

steps.action: Construct a limestone rock-physics model (VRH mineral mixing, modified Pride dry-frame model, Gassmann fluid substitution, seawater-filled connected pores) with handbook mineral moduli.
steps.quote: a modified Pride empirical model (Pride et al., 2004) was used

steps.action: Vary water content, consolidation coefficient and single-mineral matrix in the limestone model to check the trends and bounds of P-impedance (Figure 8).
steps.quote: the variation in the elastic parameters with water content and consolidation coefficient was verified.

steps.action: Fix the consolidation coefficient within a range set by experience, choosing the value that matches the observed P-impedance range.
steps.quote: selected the most appropriate value according to the actual P-wave impedance value range.

steps.action: Construct a basalt rock-physics model with the Kuster-Toksoz model, using spherical pores (aspect ratio 1) and penny cracks (0.1) filled with seawater.
steps.quote: the KT model was selected to calculate the bulk and shear modulus of basalt.

steps.action: Vary water content and the sphere-to-penny-crack ratio in the basalt model and check how P-impedance responds (Figure 9).
steps.quote: the law in which P-wave impedance varies with the two was verified (Figure 9)

steps.action: Choose a best sphere-to-crack pore ratio by matching the modelled to the inverted P-impedance.
steps.quote: we chose a best value for the ratio of spherical pores and coin-shaped pores

steps.action: Invert P-impedance for mineral contents and porosity with a genetic algorithm (population 400, 20 generations, penalty function in the fitness).
steps.quote: The population number was set to 400, and the number of iterations was set to 20.

steps.action: Compare porosity from the genetic algorithm with measured porosity at the sedimentary (IODP 363) and basalt (ODP 192) sites (Figure 10; eight boreholes, p. 737).
steps.quote: The results obtained from the inversion matched well with the actual data at the sites (Figure 10).

steps.action: Compute the free-water content profile assuming water saturation of 1, downsampling the input 1:10 for speed and converting time to depth (Figure 11).
steps.quote: we processed the input data on a scale of 1:10.

steps.action: Identify a high water-content layer (about 300 kg/m3, up to about 2 km thick, extending about 25 km) in the shallow basalt of the subducting plate, and argue it is real because it matches a low-impedance anomaly (Figures 12 and 13).
steps.quote: This corresponds well to the low P-wave impedance anomaly in the inverted P-wave impedance profile, and therefore, this feature may be real.

steps.action: Propose that the anomaly reflects pore water penetrating down faults and cracks, citing a local anomaly at the slab top.
steps.quote: this may be caused by the penetration of pore water down faults and cracks.

steps.action: Compute the free-water flux from the water-content profile at the maximum cited subduction rate of 12.5 cm/yr: 158 Tg/Ma/m in total (53.724 in sediment, 105.06 in basalt).
steps.quote: In this paper, we took 12.5 cm/year for estimation.

steps.action: Compare the flux with published global-average pore-water fluxes (Moore & Vrolijk 1992; Hacker 2008; Rea & Ruff 1996) and find New Britain higher.
steps.quote: Compared to the average value of the global pore water flux as calculated by previous researchers

steps.action: Attribute the higher flux to the steeper subduction angle at New Britain, without testing it.
steps.quote: this is likely due to the observation that its subduction angle is higher than is that of many subducting plates.

steps.action: Compare with New Britain-specific estimates (Jarrard 2003, 14.7 Tg/Ma/m; von Huene & Scholl 1991, 46.2 Tg/Ma/m): sediment flux is similar, basalt flux is higher.
steps.quote: The data for sedimentary rocks are similar to the previous study.

steps.action: Explain the basalt mismatch by the saturation auxiliary (basalt saturation is likely well below 1) and reframe the estimate as an upper limit, rather than revising the inversion.
steps.quote: the water saturation of basalt pores is much less than 1

steps.action: Keep the 158 Tg/Ma/m figure as the upper limit of free-water flux into the New Britain Trench and call for follow-up work on basalt saturation.
steps.quote: The upper limit of the subducted pore fluid flux into the New Britain Trench was estimated

tree.answer: Pore/free water carried into the New Britain subduction zone; its flux is poorly quantified
No; water content is latent, inferred from seismic impedance through rock-physics models
Estimate the 2D free-water distribution and flux
No rival hypotheses; only prior published flux estimates
Conditions found: one existing seismic line plus distant boreholes
Partly: parameter sensitivity plots and a borehole porosity comparison; no uncertainty on the flux
Flux estimate kept as an upper limit (saturation = 1)

end.claim: The free-water flux subducted into the New Britain Trench is estimated at 158 Tg/Ma/m (53.724 Tg/Ma/m in sediment, 105.06 Tg/Ma/m in basalt), an upper limit assuming full water saturation.

decisive_move.sentence: The genetic-algorithm inversion of the CSSI impedance profile through the limestone and basalt rock-physics models produces the water-content profile on which the flux rests.

gates.evidence: The seismic line (2017) and the borehole logs existed before the study and were not acquired under a hypothesis. The genetic-algorithm porosity faced a comparison with borehole porosity that it could have failed (Figure 10, p. 745-746). The flux estimate itself was only compared with prior estimates; when the basalt value mismatched, it was protected by the saturation assumption and reframed as an upper limit (p. 748). Model parameters (consolidation coefficient, pore ratio) were tuned to the inverted impedance after seeing the data (p. 743, 745).

imports.item: Genetic algorithm (natural selection, crossover, mutation) used to invert impedance for mineral contents and porosity

novelty_claims.quote: This paper presents a new method for estimating fluid flux.
reveals the potential for the direct estimation of the 2D structural distribution of water content using geophysical survey data.
Previous studies examining impedance in this area are more qualitative than quantitative and assess S-wave rather than P-wave

limits:
1. Uncertainty. No uncertainty or resolution is given for the flux. The status estimate_with_resolution is applied loosely; strictly, only a point value framed as an upper limit is reported.
2. Data coverage. A single 2D profile is used. Only one well (L'Etoile No. 1) is near the line. The ODP/IODP holes used to build and check the models lie far away (Figure 1). The holes are shallow (under 400 m in sediment, or reaching only the basalt top), so there is no deep control.
3. Borehole check. Inference: the borehole porosity comparison (Figure 10) appears to use site impedances and the same data that informed the models, so it is likely in-sample. It is not a test of the seismic-derived water content along line 200.
4. Free parameters. The consolidation coefficient and the sphere-to-crack ratio were tuned to the inverted impedance, and their final values are not reported. The genetic algorithm is stopped at 20 generations, with no convergence or rerun test reported.
5. Circularity. Inference: the argument that the water anomaly is real because it matches the low-impedance anomaly is circular, since water content is derived from impedance.
6. Saturation. Water saturation is assumed to be 1. The discussion's statement on basalt saturation is internally confusing (it says it may make the basalt flux 'much less' than previous studies, while the basalt flux is reported as higher).
7. Untested hypotheses. The fault-conduit hypothesis (p. 746) and the subduction-angle explanation (p. 748) are proposed but not tested.
8. Sub-claims:
- The high water-content layer in the shallow basalt is at best best_explanation (weakly supported).
- The sediment flux agreeing with prior work is a comparison only.
9. Missing documents. No review file was supplied, so nothing is known about review-forced changes.
10. Composition. none_fits because the walk is a method-chain estimation from existing data, with no rivals, no repeated natural cases and no new instrument.

disagreements.target: Global average pore-water flux estimates (Moore & Vrolijk 1992; Hacker 2008; Rea & Ruff 1996)
disagreements.support: The paper's New Britain flux (158 Tg/Ma/m) exceeds the global averages (20.2-40.4 Tg/Ma/m), which it attributes to a steeper subduction angle without testing this.
disagreements.quote: Compared to the average value of the global pore water flux as calculated by previous researchers

disagreements.target: New Britain igneous-crust pore water estimates (Jarrard 2003; von Huene & Scholl 1991)
disagreements.support: The basalt flux of 105.06 Tg/Ma/m is higher than the prior 14.7 and 46.2 Tg/Ma/m; the paper explains this by the saturation assumption and calls its value an upper limit.
disagreements.quote: however, the free water content of basalt is higher than previous estimates.

disagreements.target: Previous impedance studies in the Solomon region ( [...] . 1993; Day et al. 2015; Phinney et al. 1999)
disagreements.support: The paper argues that CSSI with well-log constraints gives a quantitative P-wave impedance result, where earlier work was qualitative and S-wave based.
disagreements.quote: Previous studies examining impedance in this area are more qualitative than quantitative and assess S-wave rather than P-wave
